L182@P6: A. Methodology
L183@P6: Our study exploits high-frequency variation in prices in Treasury futures around Treasury auctions to measure shifts in investor demand for U.S. safe assets. While institutional details of these
L184@P6: auctions are well-documented in Ray et al. (2024), for the purpose of this paper, the following
L185@P6: characteristics about Treasury auctions are worth highlighting. First, Treasury auctions are frequent and pre-announced events at which the U.S. Treasury offers newly issued debt to the public.
L186@P6: Over our sample period, which spans 2002 to 2018, we observe 944 auctions, resulting in approximately one event per week, on average. Second, the maturity of offered contracts varies across
L187@P6: auction dates. Contracts include 2-, 3-, 5-, and 7-year notes and 10- and 30-year bonds. The
L188@P6: frequency of debt issuance varies over time and across contracts. During our sample, contracts
L189@P6: with maturities of 2-years are most frequently issued (36%), followed by 7- to 10-year notes and
L190@P6: bonds (31%), 3- to 5- year notes (20%), and 30-year bonds (13%). Third, a variety of different
L191@P6-7: 6market participants with different objectives actively engages in auctions by submitting competitive and non-competitive bids. The difference between these types of bids are relevant for our
L192@P7: identification strategy. Noncompetitive bidder are limited to $5 million per bidder and subject
L193@P7: to the terms settled at the auction. Competitive bids, in contrast, are associated with specific
L194@P7: amounts that market participants aim to purchase. The submission cut-off times for the different
L195@P7: types of bids varies, and competitive bids usually can be submitted until the closing time. Lastly,
L196@P7: the vast majority of auctions take place at 13:00 (96% of all auctions in our sample), while the
L197@P7: remaining number of auctions takes place at 11:30 or 11:00. Figure 1 puts the point in time of
L198@P7: auctions into perspective relative to other intraday events in financial markets, and which have

L235@P8: maturity of the issued debt instruments; and their CUSIP codes.

L256@P9: close to two-thirds of the average total daily turnover in foreign exchange markets (BIS (2022)).
L257@P9: We transform the tick-by-tick data from LSEG in the following way. We obtain the best bid
L258@P9: and ask quote recorded to the nearest even second. After applying a number of filters to correct
L259@P9: the data for outliers, the price at each five-minute tick is obtained by linearly interpolating from
L260@P9: the average of the bid and ask quotes for the two closest ticks. If no quote was submitted during
L261@P9: a specific interval, we fill the gap with the most recent available price.
L262@P9: Following previous studies (see, e.g., Andersen et al., 2003) we exclude quotes that are submitted on days that are associated with low trading activity. For example. we remove all quotes on
L263@P9: weekends between Friday 17:00 and Sunday 17:05 (Eastern Time, ET). Similarly, we drop quotes
L264@P9: around fixed holidays, i.e., Christmas (24 to 26 December), New Year (31 December to 2 January),
L265@P9: and 4 July, and around flexible holidays, such as Good Friday, Easter Monday, Memorial Day,
L266@P9: Labor Day, and Thanksgiving (including the day after).
L267@P9: We define currencies as U.S. dollar per foreign currencies, i.e., an increase of the exchange rate
L268@P9: (i.e., positive returns) reflects an appreciation of the foreign currency vis-`a-vis the U.S. dollar.
L269@P9: Lastly, we obtain daily data on zero-coupon bonds from Bloomberg for the G9 foreign bond
L270@P9: markets and the United States. We collect fixed income instruments with maturities ranging from
L271@P9: 3-months to 30-years, providing us with detailed information on the yield curve for each of the
L272@P9: ten major economies.
